BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: Light valley rain and mountain snow will be on the way out Monday as the shortwave upper trough moves east, with minimal accumulations anticipated.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Light snow is tapering off this morning with low clouds generally lifting.
- Breezy northwesterly winds up to 35 mph will continue in the Baker Valley and Magic Valley through the evening.
- Next round of precipitation with limited accumulations passes early Sunday into early Monday.
- A generally cool and wet pattern will continue through next week, with brief dry periods on Saturday and next Tuesday.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: This low pressure system will move east by the early afternoon, leaving cooler and breezy conditions in its wake. Westerly winds will be strongest in the Magic Valley and in southern Baker County, with gusts up to 35 mph during the afternoon. Some lingering snow showers near the ID/NV border are tapering off this afternoon as well. A high pressure ridge builds in briefly behind the exiting low. Dry and cold conditions through Saturday, with fog forming in higher terrain and in sheltered valleys late Friday night. Best chances for fog formation are near Burns, Ontario, and McCall. Generally in valleys or basins with the weakest wind and higher accumulations of recent precip/snow. In the Snake Plain, weak downsloping wind overnight will hinder widespread fog, though as temps approach saturation localized fog near rivers is possible. A shortwave trough will move through the region late Sunday, bringing another quick hit of valley rain and mountain snow. Morning temperatures on Sunday will be just above freezing as precipitation arrives. Persistent cold bias in consensus guidance has allowed raw guidance to shine, which agrees with a warmer solution. This will support precip falling as rain in the Snake Plain, changing to mixed in the upper Snake Plain and foothills, and snow for Idaho highlands and the majority of Southeast Oregon. As the surface low associated with the shortwave gets quickly swallowed by the deeper Pacific low, precipitation will pass similarly quickly with limited accumulation. Generally snow accumulations of 1-2 inches and rainfall of up to 0.1 inch is forecast in Central Idaho, lower Snake Plain, and SE Oregon.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Light valley rain and mountain snow will be on the way out Monday as the shortwave upper trough moves east, with minimal accumulations anticipated. An upper-level ridge will briefly build into the region late Monday and last into mid-Tuesday, providing a short-lived drying and warming trend. Starting late Tuesday, a deep upper-level low in the Gulf of Alaska will transport a significant amount of moisture into the Pacific Northwest. The atmospheric river will mostly affect the coastal West CONUS, with model disagreement on how far east the moisture will advect. Despite disagreements on amounts, southwesterly flow aloft will bring more valley rain and mountain snow by midweek. Precipitation will mainly be in southeast Oregon and over higher terrain in southwest Idaho. Model agreement diverges significantly after Thursday, primarily on the position of an upper level low just west of Vancouver Island and the strength of a ridge of high pressure over the West Coast. The current long term forecast favors the warmer and drier scenario, which would keep the ridge of high pressure stronger and over the Intermountain West.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: We are confident that the plains will see highs in the 40s to near 50 and lows in the low/mid 20s which will continue through most of next week. These temperatures will be 5 to even 10 degrees below average- the coolest weather of the season.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Chances for light mountain snow continues through Saturday. Flurries possible from the urban corridor to the Palmer Divide on Saturday morning.
- Gusty winds and elevated to near-critical fire weather conditions this afternoon across most of the Front Range foothills and plains.
- Cooler pattern starting Saturday and lasting into next week. Another system brings the chance for more high country snow as early as Monday.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: A strong southwest jet aloft has brought gusty winds to the high country and the majority of the plains today. Gusty winds are likely to continue for the next few hours. The high country could see wind gusts of 50-60 mph with slightly higher gusts possible at the highest elevations. We expect 30-40 mph wind gusts to continue across the plains. These winds are expected to slack off in the next few hours as the upper-level flow starts to weaken gradually, but some gusty winds could be possible through late tonight at the highest elevations. Additionally, relative humidity remains at or below 20% for most of the plains south of I-76. Thus, we have had some extreme to near-critical fire weather conditions today and this threat will continue for a few more hours. Today is forecast to be the warmest day of the upcoming week with highs mainly in the 60s for the plains. Cooler air is starting to filter into the northern plains and northern metro at this hour.

Current radar shows some snow showers ongoing across the central and northern high country with visibilities briefly dropping. There is the chance for some light snow accumulations this afternoon for the high country with the Park Range being the most favored location. Only about an additional inch or two of snow seems plausible as the shortwave departs.

A cold front is progged to move through the area late this afternoon from north to south. This will usher in cooler temperatures for the week ahead. Saturday morning, we expect an increase in QG ascent as the trough moves through and moisture has slightly increased in the latest modeling. We have increased cloud cover for tomorrow, which could keep temperatures across the urban corridor right at or just above freezing. On Saturday morning into the early afternoon, snow levels drop as cold air advection continues, 700 mb temperatures cool, and weak upslope flow is expected. There is a low chance (~20%) for some light snow on the plains with about a 30% chance for the southern foothills. For the urban corridor, in particular, there is only about a 10% chance for very light accumulations given the marginal temperatures. Odds increase very slightly for the Palmer Divide. The central and southern high country have a higher chance of seeing some accumulations tomorrow morning, but only around one inch. If the ingredients can come together, some locations in the southern foothills and southern high country could get a bit more accumulation.

Saturday will be much cooler than today with temperatures struggling to reach the mid 40s for the plains. Ridging quickly moves in Saturday night into Sunday, but highs are forecast to only moderate a few degrees on Sunday afternoon. Models and ensemble guidance continue to show the potential for two different systems affecting our area next week- one at the beginning of the week and one towards the end of the week. Run-to-run and model-to-model variability remains high, so there is very low confidence in any precipitation timing/impacts. More westerly/northwesterly flow aloft means our central and southern high country are most favored, in general. Monday into early Tuesday brings the next chance for snow for the high country. The NBM does a good job of depicting that only light accumulations are expected. Some light rain and/or snow could spread onto the plains on Monday night into Tuesday morning.

We are confident that the plains will see highs in the 40s to near 50 and lows in the low/mid 20s which will continue through most of next week. These temperatures will be 5 to even 10 degrees below average- the coolest weather of the season. This forecast will be something to keep tabs on with the busy travel week ahead.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Friday...Split shortwave trough energy with the northern piece traveling across the Dakotas by suppertime, and a closed low over New Mexico. Thus, we will be in the dry sector in between.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Strong and gusty winds expected through this evening for the wind prones of southeast Wyoming.
- Isolated to scattered light snow shower activity will remain possible in Carbon, Albany, Converse, and Niobrara Counties through Saturday.
- Expect chillier temperatures this weekend into early next week with a few additional chances for light, spotty snow showers.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Precipitation activity has relaxed for the most part this afternoon in a drier environment despite the impressive morning we had, with locations such as Rawlins seeing much more snow than expected. A modest amount of instability is also noted, particularly moving to the northeast into South Dakota where a thunderstorm is seen currently. Moisture and forcing should be favorable to continue some generally light precipitation activity for our western and northern zones overnight through tomorrow morning as a secondary trough moves into the region, but into the afternoon this should finally move out as troughing begins to exit and transient ridging overspreads into Sunday. But in a post-frontal environment, expect cold temperatures as lows tomorrow morning will be widespread below freezing, with feels like temperatures into the teens and even some single digits. Highs for Saturday will be around 5 degrees below average with widespread 30's to 40's, with overnight lows into Sunday then descending into the widespread teens.

Also of note, a High Wind Warnings continue through this evening as pressure gradients have been conducive for stronger winds of 50-60 mph across our normal wind prone locations. While these should begin to relax this evening, breezy winds will continue through Saturday, finally relaxing as the pressure gradients loosen into Sunday. This should end the need for any highlights tonight, with conditions becoming chilly and drying out as we head into the end of the weekend.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Sunday...Dry with zonal flow aloft and minimal low and mid level moisture. A bit colder than Saturday with maxima in the upper 30s to lower 40s and 700 mb temperatures near -5 Celsius.

Monday...Next neutrally tilted shortwave trough approaches from western Wyoming with the flow aloft turning southwest, and increasing chances for orographic snows across our Snowy and Sierra Madre Ranges. Progressive nature of the shortwave trough aloft suggests snowfall amounts below Winter Weather Advisory criteria.

Tuesday...As the trough aloft moves eastward to the Great Plains states, our flow aloft turns northerly, with dry conditions in the wake of the perturbation. Continued near normal temperatures with highs in the mid 30s to mid 40s and 700 mb temperatures near -6 Celsius.

Wednesday...The progressive pattern, synoptically, continues with a high amplitude ridge aloft moving overhead and keeping our weather high and dry. Warmer temperatures return with ridging aloft for Wednesday through Friday.

Thanksgiving...The next shortwave trough aloft sweeps to an Idaho to Four Corners line, with southerly flow aloft over our neck of the woods. Low and mid level moisture looks sufficient for scattered orographic snows for our Snowy and Sierra Madre Ranges, and dry elsewhere. Decent day for the holiday with maxima in the 40s to lower 50s.
Friday...Split shortwave trough energy with the northern piece traveling across the Dakotas by suppertime, and a closed low over New Mexico. Thus, we will be in the dry sector in between.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: There is a vague signal of another system passing through in the latter half of next week, but cluster analysis shows a wide range of outcomes with low confidence on when wet weather would arrive, if at all.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - 2-4 more inches of snow possible throughout tonight and Saturday morning in the San Juans, central Colorado mountains, and some mountain valleys.
- Temperatures will trend downward for the weekend, with most desert valleys seeing their first freezing temperatures of the season.
- Active weather is possible through much of Thanksgiving week. Stay tuned for updates to timing and impacts as they become available.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: SNOW TO CONTINUE THROUGH SATURDAY MORNING:

Low pressure is situated over the Great Basin tonight, and as a result, modest moisture continues to flow into our region amid the southwesterly flow. This has and will continue to support scattered showers tonight and through the majority of Saturday morning. The trough axis swings through near mid-day tomorrow, quickly shutting off the tap of moisture and ending the majority of active weather in our CWA. Until then, look for another one to three tenths of liquid precipitation to fall across the San Juans, central Colorado mountains, and along US-50 (generally east of Montrose). Cooler temperatures will continue to support lower snow levels, and so with most remaining precipitation expected over mountains and mountain valleys, snow should dominate throughout the end of this event. Additional accumulations will generally be under 3 inches, though some locally higher amounts are possible on the northern slopes of the San Juans where snowfall is expected to be more persistent through the night. Otherwise, temperatures have notably dropped behind the frontal boundary which passed through today, which means overnight lows for the next several night are tracking to drop below freezing for a large swath of the region. Any valley locations which have yet to hit freezing temperatures should expect to drop below freezing as a result.

A low-amplitude ridge builds in behind the exiting trough Saturday evening into Sunday morning. Skies may clear out some during the overnight period, which would support a localized fog risk in some valleys, though the current forecast isn't overly bullish on widespread saturation at the surface. Chances for fog are highest further north in the Uinta and Yampa Basins though. By Sunday evening, upper-level flow will be turning back southwesterly ahead of another approaching trough. Moisture and upper-level support is unimpressive with this storm, so current expectations are for only light showers Sunday evening through Tuesday morning. Snow accumulations are on track to sit well below advisory level.

There is a vague signal of another system passing through in the latter half of next week, but cluster analysis shows a wide range of outcomes with low confidence on when wet weather would arrive, if at all. Though confidence is extremely low at this time, this potential storm could be impactful to Thanksgiving travel. Stay tuned over the coming days for additional updates regarding the late-week weather, especially if you are planning to travel for the holiday.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: After our Tuesday system, things look dry the rest of the week, with a marginal chance of minor precip Thursday night into Friday. The upper-level forcing is there, but the flow and moisture looks too weak at this point.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Windy with rounds of light mountain snow showers across the ContDvd tonight, spreading across the higher terrain Saturday.
- Cooler Saturday with a few light showers possible across the southeast plains.
- Below normal temperatures for Sunday into next week with fast moving systems bringing opportunities for light showers later Monday into Tuesday and again later Thursday and Friday.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Current water vapor imagery and upper air analysis has broad upper trough digging across the Great Basin with a jet rounding the system producing moderate to strong southwest flow aloft across the Rockies at this time. Water vapor imagery has drier air moving across the region, with current dew pts in the teens and 20s across much of the region, save for in the 30s and 40s across the far southeast plains at this time. Regional radars are indicating showers associated the passing jet along and west of the ContDvd at this time. Strongest winds of 65 to 75 mph over and near the Southeast Mtns and Pikes Peak region have diminished, though still seeing gusty southwest winds of the 30 to 60 mph across much of the region, as strong flow aloft continues across the Rockies. The strong downslope has also help boost temperatures into the 60s across the plains, with 40s and 50s currently across the higher terrain, save for 30s at the peaks.

For the rest of today into tonight, the upper trough continues to dig across the Great Basin through tonight, keeping moderate to strong southwest winds across the higher terrain. A slight increase in moisture ahead of the system will help to develop generally light orographic snow along the Continental Divide, especially the Eastern San Juan mtns, where a few inches will be possible overnight. Winds decouple across the lower elevations through the evening, leading to lows in the 20s and 30s across the plains, and in the teens and 20s across the higher terrain.

A baggy upper trough looks to continue across south central and southeast Colorado through the day Saturday, with generally light precipitation spreading across the higher terrain through the morning and afternoon. The quick movement of the system and limited available moisture, will limit accumulations, with a few inches possible across the Central Mtns into the Rampart Range and the Southeast Mtns. Across the Southeast Plains, a weak front will push south and west through the morning, with weak low level upslope helping to produce a few snow showers across the Palmer Dvd through the late morning and early afternoon, with mixed rain and snow showers along the Raton Mesa and southern tier through the afternoon and early evening. Little to no accumulation is expected across the plains.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: The precip should end Saturday night for most of our area, perhaps persisting in the Eastern Plains into the overnight, as the moisture and the 500mb jet pass to our southeast.

The cold front will bring much cooler conditions behind it, especially for the eastern Plains, away from the mountains where temperatures could dip 5-10 degF below normal during the day Sunday. Wind will also die down near the mountains.

Monday night into Tuesday presents our next best opportunity for rain, with a trough and a 700mb low in northeastern CO. POPs are generally below 50% along I-25, and above 50% both in the Plains and the Mountains. Precip may begin for the mountains on Monday night, moving into the I-25 corridor overnight, then beginning in the Eastern Plains by sunrise. The window for precip to occur will be brief, only a few hours in any one location. QPF total will be between 0.05 and 0.2 inches. The GFS still wants to make this more considerable of an event than the ECMWF, but ensemble members from both models lean towards the ECMWF solution, so our official forecasts are very much on the lower side. The ECMWF has a shallower wave feature, while the GFS has a more robust low pressure. Any precip that falls during night should fall as snow.

After our Tuesday system, things look dry the rest of the week, with a marginal chance of minor precip Thursday night into Friday. The upper-level forcing is there, but the flow and moisture looks too weak at this point.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: Conditions will get quiet again for Tuesday/Wednesday as a transient ridge develops. Guidance for the second half of next week is a bit more uncertain.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Snow showers linger across northern Utah overnight before drying out tomorrow.
- Freezing conditions expected tonight and tomorrow night for Zion and lower Washington county.
- Another weak storm is possible for Monday with snow as low as valley floors.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: The axis of the trough that has been bringing precipitation to northern Utah is currently just to the west of KSLC. This is bringing the coldest 700 mb temperatures (between -9 and -10C) over northern Utah with westerly flow aloft. This has kept showery activity on-and-off through much of the evening. This activity will continue, especially southeast and east of the Great Salt Lake which will provide some lake induced instability to initiate more showers overnight. These showers will be relatively brief, but as temperatures have cooled to near freezing across many locations a quick dusting of snow or graupel is possible across area roadways. Some of the hi-res guidance does want to develop a more organize band around sunrise tomorrow morning somewhere between Salt Lake City and Davis county. If this does develop then an inch or two of additional snow can't be ruled out.

High pressure redevelops over the area tomorrow which will help to bring drier conditions to the region, however temperatures will remain cooler than normal by about 5 degrees. This ridge will be short-lived as another lower amplitude trough moves into the Great Basin on Monday. 53% of ensemble members keep conditions relatively dry with this trough, while the other 47% of members bring light to moderate precipitation. With 700mb temperatures of -9C with this upcoming trough there should be enough cold air to support snow down to valley floors. Given that over 50% of members keep conditions relatively dry there is very little QPF in the 50th percentile (a few hundredths across the northern terrain), however there are some wetter members. The 90th percentile has 0.25-0.5" of QPF across northern Utah with a favored area across Weber and Davis counties as a result of the westerly flow expected with the incoming trough.

Conditions will get quiet again for Tuesday/Wednesday as a transient ridge develops. Guidance for the second half of next week is a bit more uncertain. ~50% of the members remain dry while the other 50% bring in moisture from an atmospheric river making landfall in the PNW. This moisture is ushered into northern Utah alongside northwesterly flow. This could bring appreciable moisture to the mountains of northern Utah if this pans out, so it will have to be something to watch to see which solution guidance trends towards.

2660.travel_advice: Heightened avalanche conditions on specific terrain features. Evaluate snow and terrain carefully; identify features of concern.

product.author: Chris Dickson
bottom_line: Recent remote-triggered avalanches mean you should give a wide buffer to wind-drifted slopes near and above treeline to avoid triggering an avalanche that could bury you.

Very strong winds formed thicker and stiffer slabs on leeward slopes below ridgelines and in rocky gullies in the alpine. The most dangerous slopes face the north-half of the compass where weak snow lurks under these slabs. For safer travel options, seek out wind-sheltered areas. Conditions are safer below treeline.

2745.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Jason Konigsberg
bottom_line: There isn't enough snow for avalanches on most slopes. Steer around hard drifts of snow on steep terrain features and below ridgetop in the alpine.

3046.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Kevin Studley
bottom_line: Winter has begun to embrace the West Central Mountains of Idaho. 6-12 inches of new snow has fallen between Friday the 13th and Monday the 16th. Another 6-12 inches could stack up by the end of the week. If you're traveling in the mountains this week, watch out for wind slabs 1-2 feet thick above 7,000 feet and pay attention to terrain traps.
We'll update the General Avalanche Information weekly until full-time forecasting operations begin.
hazard_discussion: From 60-degree temperatures to over a foot of new snow, the weather sure has changed quickly over the past week. A cooler and wetter weather pattern has taken shape over our region since Friday the 13th. As of Monday (16th) afternoon, some mountain locations have picked up 6-12 inches of new snow along with southerly winds gusting 20-30 MPH.
Wind Slabs
• Wind slabs could become reactive this week with over a foot of new snow and gusty winds. Wind slabs will be most sensitive just below ridgelines.
• Look for clues of wind-affected snow, such as drifts, dunes, pillows, and freshly built cornices.
• Watch for signs of instability, such as shooting cracks. If you're observing these signs, find another aspect away from wind-drifted snow.
• Strong winds and local terrain features can alter the prevailing wind direction. Pay attention to cross-loading and wind-loading on unsuspecting slopes.
Early Season Conditions
• If you're out hiking or hunting in the mountains this fall, stay tuned to changing weather conditions. Avalanches are most likely during and immediately after a storm.

• Keep in mind the adage, "If there's enough snow to ride, there's enough snow to slide". Even if there's not enough snow to bury you, a small slide over uncovered logs, rocks, and brush would not be a fun way to start the season.
• Stay up to date on mountain weather with our WEATHER tab, where you'll find webcams, weather stations, and weather forecasting tools.
Check Your Winter Gear

• Beacons, shovels, probes, airbags. Run through all your gear and make sure it's functioning properly. Does your transceiver or airbag need any firmware updates? Look for cracks, defects, or corroded batteries. Make it fun with your friends and do a pre-season gear check with your winter travel companions.
Continuing Education
• Check out the Education tab on our website to sign up for avalanche courses this winter (COURSES ).
• Stay tuned to our EVENTS pages for other local happenings with the winter community.
• Interested in attending a snow and avalanche workshop (SAW)? Check out A3's WEBSITE for a list of events.
Observations
• Keep an eye on our observation page HERE

• If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation HERE. Early season observations help forecasters and the public alike. A simple photo and/or weather observation helps paint the picture of where snow is and where it is not.

Yeah, that's right: the Payette Avalanche Center has a new website. Browse around before the snow starts flying. We're also on the Avy App. You can search for "Avy: Avalanche & Weather Info" in your app store on your mobile device.

2755.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Chris Dickson
bottom_line: Most slopes are generally safe from avalanches. You might be able to trigger a small avalanche where you encounter stiff, wind-drifted snow below ridgelines, on lee slopes, and around rocky outcrops in the alpine.
